I'll count SUD co-occurrence by grouping over the top-level substance categories, using the concept hierarchy to roll up all subtypes (dependence, abuse, use disorder) per substance.

arguments.sql_query:
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%alcohol%' THEN 'Alcohol'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%nicotine%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%tobacco%' THEN 'Nicotine/Tobacco'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%cannabis%' THEN 'Cannabis'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%cocaine%' THEN 'Cocaine'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%opioid%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%opiate%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%heroin%' THEN 'Opioid'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%amphetamine%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%methamphetamine%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%stimulant%' THEN 'Amphetamine/Stimulant'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%sedative%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%hypnotic%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%anxiolytic%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%benzodiazepine%' THEN 'Sedative/Hypnotic'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%hallucinogen%' THEN 'Hallucinogen'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%inhalant%' THEN 'Inhalant'
    ELSE 'Other/polysubstance'
  END AS substance_class,
  COUNT(DISTINCT co.person_id) AS n_bipolar_with_sud
FROM omop.condition_occurrence co
JOIN omop.concept sc ON co.condition_concept_id = sc.concept_id
JOIN omop.concept_ancestor ca_sud ON co.condition_concept_id = ca_sud.descendant_concept_id
WHERE co.person_id IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT co2.person_id
    FROM omop.condition_occurrence co2
    JOIN omop.concept_ancestor ca ON co2.condition_concept_id = ca.descendant_concept_id
    WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 436665
  )
  AND ca_sud.ancestor_concept_id = 436954
GROUP BY
  CASE
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%alcohol%' THEN 'Alcohol'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%nicotine%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%tobacco%' THEN 'Nicotine/Tobacco'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%cannabis%' THEN 'Cannabis'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%cocaine%' THEN 'Cocaine'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%opioid%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%opiate%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%heroin%' THEN 'Opioid'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%amphetamine%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%methamphetamine%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%stimulant%' THEN 'Amphetamine/Stimulant'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%sedative%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%hypnotic%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%anxiolytic%' OR sc.concept_name LIKE '%benzodiazepine%' THEN 'Sedative/Hypnotic'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%hallucinogen%' THEN 'Hallucinogen'
    WHEN sc.concept_name LIKE '%inhalant%' THEN 'Inhalant'
    ELSE 'Other/polysubstance'
  END
ORDER BY n_bipolar_with_sud DESC

Of **24,194 bipolar patients**, **8,793 (36.3%)** have at least one substance-use diagnosis. Here is the co-occurrence breakdown from the EHR, with the neurotransmitter interpretation.

## Co-occurring substance-use diagnoses in bipolar disorder

| Substance class | Patients | % of bipolar cohort |
|---|---|---|
| Nicotine/Tobacco | 4,875 | 20.1% |
| Other/polysubstance | 3,199 | 13.2% |
| Alcohol | 2,960 | 12.2% |
| Amphetamine/Stimulant | 1,809 | 7.5% |
| Opioid | 1,440 | 6.0% |
| Cannabis | 1,176 | 4.9% |
| Cocaine | 1,004 | 4.2% |
| Sedative/Hypnotic | 103 | 0.4% |
| Hallucinogen | 93 | 0.4% |
| Inhalant | 20 | 0.1% |

(Categories overlap — polysubstance patients count in multiple rows.)

## Neurotransmitter systems that may link them

The clustering isn't random: the substances that co-occur most sit on the same circuits implicated in bipolar mood regulation.

- **Dopamine (mesolimbic reward)** — the common thread. Manic states involve dopaminergic hyperactivity, and nicotine, alcohol, stimulants (amphetamine/cocaine), and opioids all converge on dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens/VTA. This shared reward-circuit dysregulation is the leading explanation for why the top substances here (nicotine, alcohol, stimulants, cocaine) are exactly the dopaminergic ones. Stimulants can also directly precipitate or mimic manic episodes.
- **GABA / glutamate (excitatory–inhibitory balance)** — alcohol and sedative/hypnotics are GABA-A agonists; withdrawal produces glutamatergic rebound. Bipolar disorder itself shows glutamate/GABA imbalance, and several mood stabilizers (valproate, lamotrigine) act here — a mechanistic overlap that can drive "self-medication" of mixed/agitated states.
- **Endogenous opioid & endocannabinoid systems** — opioid and cannabis use interact with mood, impulsivity, and stress-reward signaling; the endocannabinoid system modulates both dopamine tone and emotional regulation.
- **Serotonin & noradrenaline** — broadly dysregulated in mood disorders and modulated by alcohol and stimulants, contributing to shared impulsivity and affective instability.

**Two non-exclusive frameworks** explain the pattern: *self-medication* (using substances to blunt or lift mood states) and *shared vulnerability* (overlapping genetics and reward-circuit/dopaminergic dysfunction predisposing to both). The strong nicotine and alcohol signals here are consistent with both.
